newsitem.title: USA: NY Assembly members attack Gov property tax plan.
newsitem.headline: NY Assembly members attack Gov property tax plan.

text.p: A coalition of New York State Assembly members on Monday attacked Gov George Pataki's plan to cut school property taxes for New York homeowners, saying that instead it would result in higher tax rates.

The lawmakers said that they would continue to push for their own bill to reduce property taxes, explaining it would give low- and middle-income residents a tax credit of up to $500, based on the property taxes that they pay localities.

"We appreciate the fact that the governor has announced his plan to reduce property taxes in the state but we have had a workable plan on the table for the last two years. Unfortunately the goveror's plan will substantially raise the property taxes of almost every residential taxpayer in the state," said Richard Brodsky, D-Westchester, in prepared remarks.

Pataki, who has made cutting taxes one of the chief selling points of his Administration, over the weekend unveiled a five-year, $3.4 billion plan to reduce school property taxes while raising school funding.

The governor also has accelerated to January the last part of a three-year, nearly $3.9 billion cut in income taxes. State aid has climbed to $44.6 billion in fiscal year 1996-1997 from $42.5 billion in the previous fiscal year, according to CHANGE-NY, a taxpayer group that supports Pataki's new plan for property tax relief.
Yet school property taxes have risen faster than the rate of inflation in the 1980s and the early 1990s.

A spokesman for Pataki said that the Assemblyman's Westchester constituents would be better-served by the governor's proposal, which aims to cut residential school property taxes by $1.7 billion when fully phased-in over four years.

"Maybe when he (Brodsky) takes a closer look at the proposal he won't be so quick to file another mistake-riddled press release. The governor's plan will reduce property taxes, particularly for people in Westchester County, significantly," said Mike McKeon, the governor's press secretary.
